Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

A chapel painted on a flat wall

Describe

Masaccio painted this fresco in Florence around 1425. Follow the lines of the ceiling: where do they meet?

Construction

They meet near the eye height of a person standing in the church: the flat wall opens into a chapel that is not there.

Critical

The space is built for one standing viewer. Who is that ideal viewer, and where must everyone else stand?

Image: Masaccio’s Holy Trinity fresco, about 1425: a painted barrel vault that recedes to a single vanishing point at the viewer’s eye level.

Masaccio, trinità · Masaccio · Public domain · Source

  • Often called the earliest surviving fresco in full linear perspective.

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

The picture as an open window

In 1435 Leon Battista Alberti told painters to treat the picture as a window. Erwin Panofsky describes the method as a flat cut through the cone of sight.

I imagine the picture – in accord with the “window” definition – as a planar cross section through the so-called visual pyramid

(Panofsky 1991, 28)

Image: Perspective construction plate from Alberti Della pittura showing vanishing-point geometry

Della Pittura Alberti perspective vanishing point · Leon Battista Alberti · Rights under review · Source

  • Panofsky paraphrases the Albertian procedure in the first person.
  • The grid floor is the measuring tool.

Alberti’s window: a cut through the visual pyramid

  • Station point, rays, plane, image: four words to keep.

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

One still eye, one measurable space

Central perspective assumes a viewer with one eye who never moves. In exchange, lived space becomes a space you can measure tile by tile, as Piero della Francesca did.

In a sense, perspective transforms psychophysiological space into mathematical space.

(Panofsky 1991, 31)

Panofsky calls the two assumptions — one still eye, a flat cut — bold abstractions from real vision.

Image: Piero della Francesca’s Flagellation: a measured architectural space with a tiled floor, three robed men in the foreground and a scene deep behind.

Piero - The Flagellation · Piero della Francesca · Public domain · Source

  • Panofsky 1991, 29: 'we see with a single and immobile eye'.
  • Two moving eyes and a curved retina are what the rule leaves out.

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

Not whether perspective, but which

Panofsky called perspective a symbolic form: each culture builds space its own way. In Edo Japan, uki-e prints borrowed Western perspective for theatre streets full of kimono.

it is essential to ask of artistic periods and regions not only whether they have perspective, but also which perspective they have

(Panofsky 1991, 40)

Image: Japanese uki-e woodblock print by Utagawa Toyoharu: an Edo theatre district drawn in imported Western perspective, crowds in kimono receding along the street.

Perspective Picture (Uki-e)- Theater District at Dawn on Opening Day of the Kabuki Season (IA mma perspective picture ukie theater district at dawn on opening day of the 36669) · Utagawa Toyoharu · Public domain · Source

  • Uki-e ('floating pictures') appear in the 1730s–40s; Toyoharu is a later master.
  • Boden would call this a combinational move.

Three kinds of creative move

  • Boden 2004, 1: creativity = new, surprising, valuable.
  • Boden 2004, 4: conceptual spaces include 'fashions in couture'.

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

Perspective cuts both ways

Holbein's Ambassadors (1533) hides a stretched skull that reads only from one oblique spot. The rule that orders space also makes the image depend on where you stand.

For perspective is by nature a two-edged sword

(Panofsky 1991, 67)

Image: Holbein’s The Ambassadors, 1533: two richly dressed men beside instruments; a stretched skull across the floor becomes legible only from one oblique point.

Hans Holbein the Younger - The Ambassadors - Google Art Project · Hans Holbein the Younger · Public domain · Source

  • Objective rule, subjective viewpoint: Panofsky 1991, 67.
  • Ask a student to find the skull's point on a phone screen.

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

Who holds the grid, who is measured?

In Dürer's woodcut a clothed man looks through a grid at a reclining, half-draped woman. Perspective is also a relation of power between the one who looks and the one looked at.

Fashion images inherit the grid: lens, pose, crop.

Image: Dürer’s woodcut: a draughtsman looks through a gridded frame at a reclining, partly draped woman and copies her onto squared paper.

Draughtsman Making a Perspective Drawing of a Reclining Woman MET DP816489 · Albrecht Dürer · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • From the 1538 edition of Dürer's treatise on measurement.
  • Link to the dignity guide: who chooses the pose?

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

Perfect perspective still cannot fit a dress

A robe à la française of about 1765 gets its width from panniers underneath. Any number of perfect views can agree while the under-structure stays invisible.

Construction draws space. Only I.6 tests how a volume behaves on a body.

Image: A silk robe à la française of about 1765 on a mannequin, its skirt widened at the hips by panniers.

Robe à la Française MET DT5011 · The Metropolitan Museum of Art (photograph); unknown French maker (gown) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Bridge: multi-view is a question about volume, not a proof of fit.
  • Optional: show the perspective-kit P6 multiview diagram from the lesson.

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

Recall check

Alone, from memory, three minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. What did Alberti compare the picture to, in 1435?
  2. What two things does central perspective assume?
  3. What is a symbolic form?
  4. Why is perspective a two-edged sword?
  5. Why can't perfect views prove a dress fits?

Course geometric background · threshold · #c378606cc29b · Original course SVG

Answers:

  • An open window.
  • One still eye; a flat cut through the visual pyramid.
  • A cultural way of building space: which perspective, not whether.
  • It orders space objectively but depends on one viewer's position.
  • Volume can come from hidden structure, ease and cloth behaviour.

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

Exercise 1 · One eye, one step

Fix your phone at one eye position, turn on the camera grid and photograph a garment on a chair. Move one step sideways and shoot again.

Set-up in the lesson

Pair the two shots with one sentence: what changed in the garment's volume when only the eye moved?

Image: Piero’s Madonna del Parto: a pregnant Virgin in a blue gown opened at the front, framed by two angels holding back a tent.

Madonna del parto piero della Francesca · Piero della Francesca · Public domain · Source

  • Phone on a stack of books keeps the eye still.
  • Grid lines = Alberti's veil.

Volume and depth · Lecture B of 3

Exercise 2 · Same garment, two spaces

Draw the same garment twice: once in central perspective from one fixed point, once as a scroll seen while you walk past it.

Both drawing rules in the lesson

Upload both drawings and name the symbolic form each one assumes: whose eye, standing where?

Image: Detail of the Qingming scroll: a bridge crowded with people, boats and shops, drawn from a high, travelling viewpoint without one vanishing point.

Along the River During the Qingming Festival (detail of original) · Zhang Zeduan · Public domain · Source

  • The scroll is read by moving: no one station point.
  • Sketchbook or tablet; no AI.
